notes:
I've written notes on all 22 verses below, but some are thin. The tools kept failing and then hit their usage limit partway through. So most notes come from search-result extracts of a few commentary pages, not from whole pages I read.

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Not reached:** the full Gill and Ellicott pages, Wesley's own notes, Precept Austin, the NET Bible notes beyond verses 5 and 7, and any Reformed, Lutheran, Pentecostal or Catholic page dealing with this psalm verse by verse.
- **Too thin to use:** the Orthodox (oca.org) page I found doesn't mention this psalm.
- **Not found:** anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm, so I've left those out.
- **Weak verses:** 10, 14 and 16 have only brief notes.

Where I name a writer quoted on another page (for example Kidner or Calvin on a StudyLight page), the URL is the page where I found it.

---

## Introduction / Title ("for remembrance")
- Kidner, quoted by Guzik: in Scripture, for God to "remember" is for God to act. So the title means setting a situation before God that needs His help. Guzik says no one can tie the psalm to a definite event in David's life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Matthew Henry calls this a penitential psalm, full of grief from start to finish. David seems to be sick, abandoned by friends and attacked by enemies. Henry says times of sickness are times to bring our sins to mind and be humbled. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_038.cfm
- Spurgeon thinks guessing the occasion is foolish. The psalm may come from David's own sickness, or he may have written it for sick and slandered believers in general. An older writer Spurgeon quotes thinks David believed he was dying and was bringing to mind his sin with Bathsheba. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm
- The Biblical Illustrator (preaching Spurgeon's material) applies "remembrance" widely: remember God's past help, your enemies, and God's patience and grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-38.html
- Barnes thinks the sickness made David remember his sins. He rejects reading the psalm as being about a national disaster rather than one person's illness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-38.html

## v. 1
- Spurgeon reads it as: correct me as a Father, but don't turn the rod into a sword, and don't treat me as an enemy or rebel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm
- Horne, quoted by Guzik: David asks God not to condemn him as a judge but to correct him as a father, so that he is changed and kept. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- The Pulpit Commentary, on the Bible Hub verse page:
  - The verse echoes Psalm 6:1.
  - David is praying for God's anger to end, rather than for the rebuke itself to stop.

  On the same page:
  - The Geneva Bible note says David isn't asking to escape God's rod, only that God would ease it enough for him to bear.
  - Another note says the punishment feels like it comes from an angry Judge rather than a loving Father.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/38-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary (StudyLight) says guilt makes a person afraid of more of God's anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html

## v. 2
- Guzik:
  - The arrows and the pressing hand are word-pictures for how deeply David felt God's displeasure.
  - On the cross Jesus took the same agony, but for our sins, not His own.
  - Guzik quotes Horne to the same effect.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Henry: God's arrows always hit their target and stay stuck until God pulls them out and heals the wound. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_038.cfm
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary compares God's correction to barbed arrows: unseen, unexpected and lasting. It applies the image to the Holy Spirit piercing the conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-18.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says to look past human causes or natural laws and see God's hand in suffering. Doing so calms resentment and fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Augustine reads the arrows as God's *words*, which kindle love rather than pain. Fixed in the heart, they make the believer long for the coming "Sabbath" rest he doesn't yet have. The page is titled Psalm 38, and its quotations match this psalm. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801038.htm

## v. 3
- Guzik:
  - The suffering may have been a real illness or injury, or the physical toll of deep spiritual depression.
  - He quotes Clarke: a real disease is described, but no one can say which.
  - David doesn't see himself as a victim, because his sin caused the crisis.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Henry: God's anger lights the fire, but David clears God of blame and takes it all on himself ("because of my sin"). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_038.cfm
- Trapp: God's anger is the immediate cause of the misery, and sin the deeper cause and "true mother" of all human misery. When the two meet in the soul, there is no rest until sin is confessed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-38.cfm
- Keil & Delitzsch: sin provokes God's anger, and God's anger causes the bodily breakdown. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/38-1.htm
- Gill (Spanish version on StudyLight): seeing his sins as the cause led David to see himself as diseased with sin all over, with nothing good in his flesh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-3.html
- Spurgeon: the Holy Spirit keeps repeating this humbling truth to remove every ground for boasting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm
- **Anglican/Methodist liturgy:** Seedbed points out that the Prayer Book confession's line "there is no health in us" comes from vv. 3 and 7. https://seedbed.com/the-grammar-of-repentance-psalm-38/

## v. 4
- Keil & Delitzsch: the sins are "heavier than I," meaning more than he can bear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/38-1.htm
- Barnes: his sins piled up like waves over his head. That could mean the sense of guilt crushed him, or that his sin led to a crushing disease. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-38.html
- Spurgeon:
  - It is good when sin feels like an unbearable load.
  - This is the cry of someone who has not yet seen the great sacrifice.

  In a sermon quoted by Guzik, he adds that such terrors are not required for salvation: many true Christians never go through them.

  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- **Anglican/Methodist liturgy:** Seedbed says the confession's words about sins being too heavy a burden to bear come from this verse. https://seedbed.com/the-grammar-of-repentance-psalm-38/

## v. 5
- Barnes:
  - The Hebrew word means to melt or run, as open sores do.
  - "Foolishness" means sin, which Scripture treats as the height of folly.
  - He takes the verse as real disease, against those who read it only as a picture.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-5.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-38.html
- Calvin (StudyLight page) says that by calling his sin "foolishness" David is not playing it down, the way hypocrites excuse themselves by pleading ignorance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-5.html
- Clarke: "foolishness" may mean sin as the cause, or the foolish choice of a moment's pleasure over health and peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-5.html
- Trapp:
  - The illness isn't named; some say leprosy, and some take it all as a picture.
  - The word means welts and running sores.
  - "Foolishness" means rash folly, probably the sin with Bathsheba.

  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-38.cfm
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible):** NET translates "because of my foolish sins," noting the Hebrew reads "from before my foolishness." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+38:5,7
- **Sin and sickness:** A Bible Hub article argues the verse is poetry about personal guilt. It does not say all disease comes from personal sin; some illness simply comes from living in a fallen world. https://biblehub.com/q/does_psalm_38_5_link_wounds_only_to_sin.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** "Caring for one's wound" means always working hard to heal one's sin. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801038.htm

## v. 6
- Horne, quoted by Guzik: as pain bends the body, guilt bends the soul toward the ground in shame and fear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- The Pulpit Commentary calls his sin a weakening, unsettling sorrow that turned life into one long agony. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** reading "bowed down even unto the end," Augustine takes "the end" to mean death. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801038.htm

## v. 7
- Barnes, cited by Guzik: the burning in the loins may mean a kidney problem such as kidney stones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Trapp says God often punishes sin "in kind," so the conscience reads a sickness as the fruit of a particular sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-38.cfm
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible):** a note gives the Hebrew as "my loins are filled with shame," with the loins as the seat of emotion. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+38:5,7

## v. 8
- Guzik: Israel's "sweet psalmist" could also honestly groan before God and others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- The Pulpit Commentary: body and mind affect each other, so his inner suffering caused physical collapse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html
- A Bible Hub article:
  - Verse 8 is the hinge of the psalm: total collapse before the turn to prayer.
  - It links the groaning to Romans 8:23–26.
  - Early church writers saw Christ's outline in the psalm.

  https://biblehub.com/q/Psalm_38_8_Human_pain_God_s_reply.htm

## v. 9
- Guzik: David addresses God as Master (*Adonai*) and hides nothing. That is the opposite of Adam and Eve's instinct to hide. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: deep groaning desires toward God are themselves works of grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- A Puritan writer quoted by Spurgeon: all our heaviness lies before God to be eased, and holy mourning shuts out worldly sorrow. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm

## v. 10
- Guzik: David felt so low that life and light were leaving him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/

## v. 11
- Guzik:
  - Friends and relatives didn't care or couldn't help.
  - He quotes Kidner: the word "plague" may have been chosen for its link with leprosy (Leviticus 13), because that is how his friends treated him.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon: it looks like leprosy but matches no known case. It is a "spiritual leprosy." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm

## v. 12
- The Pulpit Commentary: on top of friends leaving, enemies use his weakness to plot against his life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: God's correction often stirs up the scheming of the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-18.html
- The Biblical Illustrator: David's many enemies don't seem to come from rashness or sourness in his life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-38.html

## vv. 13–14
- Maclaren, quoted by Guzik, compares this to David's silence when Shimei cursed him (2 Samuel 16). He speaks to God but stays silent toward people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: this brave silence pictures Jesus' silence before Pilate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Henry (StudyLight page):
  - Taking little notice of injuries protects your own peace.
  - David wouldn't even defend himself, so it couldn't be twisted against him.
  - Silence shows trust that God will defend us; defending ourselves takes God's work out of His hands.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-18.html
- The two older writers differ on why David was silent:
  - The Pulpit Commentary says guilt left him unable to answer the false charges, which made his punishment worse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html
  - A writer quoted by Spurgeon says David points to his patience as a reason for God to pity him, and calls meekness a sign of true faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm

## v. 15
- Guzik: with nothing changed and no feeling to lean on, David still chooses by faith to say "You will answer." His suffering pushes him toward God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Henry: "for in You, O LORD, I hope" explains the silence; he relies on God to clear him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-18.html
- A writer quoted by Spurgeon says to look into your sin "hanging upon Christ," like a man lowering himself into a pit on a rope. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm

## v. 16
- Guzik: David appeals to God partly so his enemies won't gloat over him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/

## v. 17
- Henry: David mourns his own weakness. He was close to complaining against God and losing his temper at his attackers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-18.html
- Trapp reads "ready to halt" as being close to behaving badly and spoiling a good cause. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-38.cfm
- Coffman: he is at the end of his strength, and unless God helps now he is lost. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-18.html

## v. 18
- Guzik: in other psalms David claims to be innocent, but not here. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Henry says repentance needs two things:
  - Specific, full confession to God.
  - Real sorrow for having dishonoured God.

  True repentance also makes us patient under unfair criticism.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-18.html
- Trapp notes Aben Ezra's view that David confessed to visitors so they would pray for him (James 5:16). Trapp prefers that he confessed to God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-38.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary: confession and repentance are the only way back to the favour of God and people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html

## v. 19
- Spurgeon, reading the KJV ("mine enemies are lively, and they are strong"): however weak the believer is, the world, the flesh and the devil are never short of energy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary: he notes how strong and many his enemies are, and that they hate him for turning *from* sin, not for his sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-38.html

## v. 20
- Spurgeon:
  - This doesn't contradict his confession. A person can be guilty before God and still innocent of wronging others.
  - Hatred for doing right is "homage which vice renders to virtue."

  An older writer he quotes says David made enemies by being careful to be holy.

  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm
- Barnes: the sickness came from God because of David's sin, but people attacked him because he followed God. That was persecution. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-38.html
- A note on the Bible Hub verse page reads the psalm as David pleading innocent of his enemies' charges while confessing to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/38-1.htm

## vv. 21–22
- Guzik:
  - The psalm ends without relief, only urgent pleas.
  - David's worst trial seems to be feeling that God is absent, more than his body or his friends.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/
- Spurgeon on "O Lord my salvation":
  - Whoever has God has salvation now.
  - Faith already begins giving God glory for the mercy it expects.
  - In heaven we'll see we had no trial too many.

  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps038.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Augustine says Christ spoke "My God, why have You forsaken Me?" in the person of the "first man" (Adam), not because the Father actually abandoned Him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801038.htm

---

## Where views differ (whole psalm)
- **Is the sickness a punishment for a specific sin?**
  - Barnes (an American Presbyterian) warns that the sick often wrongly think their illness punishes a *particular* sin. Sickness falls on the righteous too, so we shouldn't jump to that conclusion. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-38.html
  - Trapp (an English Puritan) says God often punishes sin "in kind." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-38.cfm
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) takes it plainly: some sin made David very sick. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/38-3.html
- **Real illness or a picture?** Barnes and Clarke see real disease. Trapp says some take it all as a picture. An older writer quoted by Spurgeon calls it "spiritual leprosy." (URLs above)
- **Lutheran:** a 1517.org article lists Psalm 38 among the seven penitential psalms, long linked with Lent. It says Luther valued them as God-given words for confessing sin and trusting His promise. https://www.1517.org/articles/preaching-law-and-gospel-repentance-and-faith-from-the-penitential-psalms-in-lent
- **Methodist and Anglican:** Seedbed traces the Prayer Book confession back to vv. 3–4 and 7. https://seedbed.com/the-grammar-of-repentance-psalm-38/
- **Baptist:** Spurgeon says this depth of terror is not required for salvation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-38/

## Catholic and church history
- The penitential psalms were set apart for confession from Origen's and Augustine's time, and Pope Innocent III ordered them recited in Lent. https://www.gotquestions.org/penitential-psalms.html
- In the Middle Ages each penitential psalm was linked with one of the deadly sins, and Psalm 38 with gluttony. https://www.1517.org/articles/preaching-law-and-gospel-repentance-and-faith-from-the-penitential-psalms-in-lent
